description: Welcome to our clan! I'm a cyber security student and game dev enthusiast looking to expand our squad for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our current skill tree includes ethical hacking, 3D graphics, and video editing. We are actively recruiting new clan members who have leveled up in software development, data analysis, or UI/UX design. If you're a team player ready to grind, solve complex missions, and build something epic, join our guild. Let's conquer this hackathon!
summary:
We developed Mars Base: Lost Mission, a 2.5D browser-based Mars base restoration and exploration game designed for children aged 9–12. Built with lightweight HTML5 Canvas, CSS3, and JavaScript, it runs smoothly at ~93 FPS in any web browser without installation.

Addressing the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, players spend 3 Mars Days (Sols) reviving an abandoned Martian station. They clean dust off solar panels, harvest hydroponic potatoes, extract subsurface water, produce oxygen via MOXIE, and drive a 6-wheeled Mars Rover beyond a decompressed airlock. Along the way, four base specialists and an interactive Rover panel share facts backed by real NASA missions—including ISS Veggie, Mars 2020 Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight, Phoenix, MRO, and Opportunity—rewarding players with NASA Data Points on a Mission Report Card and Top 10 Leaderboard.

This project is important because it transforms complex NASA planetary science and Martian survival challenges—such as perchlorate soil, 610 Pa atmospheric pressure, cosmic radiation, and dust storms—into intuitive, hands-on STEM learning for young students.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Our project, Mars Base: Lost Mission, is a 2.5D browser-based Mars base restoration, survival, and exploration game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Abandoned but not Forgotten") and tailored for children aged 9–12. Players begin on an interactive 3D-rendered Mars start screen where they customize their astronaut name and choose from 7 neon color badges. Over the course of 3 Mars Days (Sols), players bring an abandoned Martian research station back to life by:

• Restoring Power & Life Support: Cleaning Martian dust off 6 solar panels, harvesting hydroponic potatoes in the Greenhouse, extracting subsurface water in the Water Room, and producing breathable oxygen in the MOXIE facility.

• Managing a 4-Slot Non-Stacking Inventory: Players collect individual items—ISS Veggie potatoes (+20 HP), purified Mars water (+15 HP), and automatically acquired NASA Exploration Modules (+100 Science Points)—complete with interactive hover tooltips.

• Exploring with a Drivable Mars Rover: After equalizing pressure through a decompressed airlock ("puff" animation), players exit the base to drive a 6-wheeled Perseverance-style Mars Rover across rocky terrain and inspect real rover engineering specs.

• Learning from Real NASA Missions: Four base specialists (Botanist Emir, Commander Yaren, Engineer Murat, and Scientist Teresa) and the Rover inspection modal share kid-friendly facts backed by authentic NASA mission data (ISS Veggie & APH, Kennedy Space Center, Mars 2020 Perseverance MOXIE, Curiosity REMS/SAM/RAD, MRO SHARAD, Phoenix, InSight, Opportunity, and NASA's Deep Space Network). Discovering scientific facts earns NASA Data Points tallied on a Day-3 Mission Report Card alongside a persistent Top 10 Speedrun Leaderboard.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Complex NASA mission reports and planetary science telemetry are often inaccessible to younger students. By turning real Martian engineering challenges—such as perchlorate-contaminated regolith, 610 Pa atmospheric pressure, cosmic radiation, -63°C average temperatures, and global dust storms—into hands-on gameplay, our project builds STEM literacy and systems thinking. Instead of passively reading facts, 9–12-year-old learners actively balance energy, water, food, and oxygen while discovering how NASA solves these exact problems on Mars. Because it runs directly in any web browser with zero installation, teachers and students can use it immediately in classrooms or at home.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software

• Coding Languages & Web Stack: HTML5 (<canvas>), CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+) using localStorage for persistent leaderboards and settings—built intentionally without heavy third-party game engines.

• Software & AI Development Workflow: Visual Studio Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and Claude for rapid prototyping, collision/hitbox refinement, and code optimization, alongside CapCut for gameplay video production and custom .mp3/.wav audio integration (ambient soundtrack, airlock decompression, footsteps, Martian sand, solar cleaning, and achievement sound effects).

• Hardware: Developed and tested on an Asus TUF Gaming A16 (AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070, 32GB RAM), while engineered to maintain a smooth ~93 FPS on low-spec school and classroom computers.

Creativity & Key Design Factors

• Creativity: Rather than treating "Abandoned but not Forgotten" purely as a narrative backdrop, we designed an interactive loop where forgotten space infrastructure is revived through real NASA science—rewarding curiosity with in-game NASA Data Points, custom audio feedback, and Rover surface exploration.

• Factors Considered:

1. Age Appropriateness (Ages 9–12): Clear Turkish interface with authentic NASA source tags, intuitive controls, and a balanced energy system that prevents frustration while teaching resource management.

2. Performance & Accessibility: Cached offscreen canvas textures, pedestal-aligned precision hitboxes, and anti-clipping vehicle physics ensure lag-free play (~93 FPS) on standard school laptops.

3. Scientific Integrity: Every dialogue option and Rover specification was cross-checked against official NASA mission parameters so players learn accurate planetary science while having fun.
